title: David Lynch
summary: American filmmaker, painter and musician (1946–2025) who made the ordinary feel haunted.
characteristics: Dream logic: scenes that feel like memories you can't place
The uncanny hiding inside ordinary places — suburbs, diners, small towns
Low, droning sound design that keeps you on edge
Saturated reds, velvet curtains, flickering light

examples.title: Blue Velvet (1986)
examples.detail: White picket fences hiding something rotten.

examples.title: Twin Peaks (1990–91, 2017)
examples.detail: A TV murder mystery that turned into a dream.

whyItMatters: Lynch proves discomfort can be seductive. Naming him tells a collaborator you want unease that's beautiful, not just shocking.

title: Juergen Teller
summary: German photographer (b. 1964) whose raw, direct-flash pictures made fashion look unposed and a little awkward.
characteristics: On-camera flash aimed straight at the subject
Unretouched skin, awkward poses, deadpan humor
Everyday locations instead of polished studios

examples.title: Go-Sees (1999)
examples.detail: Portraits of young models who knocked on his studio door — unglamorous and honest.

examples.title: Marc Jacobs campaigns (late 1990s–2010s)
examples.detail: A long collaboration that made luxury ads feel like candid snaps.

examples.title: Woo! (ICA London, 2013)
examples.detail: A retrospective that showed how funny and blunt his flash can be.

whyItMatters: Teller is the reference for 'make it look caught, not produced.' Show his work when you want flash that feels honest, not glossy.

title: Francis Bacon
summary: Irish-born British painter (1909–1992) whose smeared, twisting figures made the body look raw and anxious.
characteristics: Faces and bodies smeared and twisted mid-motion
Figures trapped in glass boxes or outlined 'cages'
Flat, saturated grounds — orange, violet, deep green

examples.title: Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion (1944)
examples.detail: The triptych that made him famous: snarling creatures on burnt orange.

examples.title: Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X (1953)
examples.detail: The 'screaming pope', a portrait dissolving into streaks.

examples.title: Three Studies of Lucian Freud (1969)
examples.detail: A triptych of his friend that set an auction record in 2013.

whyItMatters: If distortion pulls you in, Bacon is the root: he shows how bending a body can say more than drawing it straight.

title: Michel Gondry
summary: French director (b. 1963) known for handmade, in-camera visual tricks and dreamlike stories.
era: Music videos from the 1990s, feature films from the 2000s
characteristics: Practical effects built by hand instead of CGI
Cardboard, felt and craft materials on screen
Loops and repetition that feel like dreams
A playful tone with melancholy underneath

examples.title: Björk — 'Human Behaviour' (1993)
examples.detail: A fairy-tale forest with a giant bear.

examples.title: The White Stripes — 'Fell in Love with a Girl' (2002)
Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004)
examples.detail: Memories erased with in-camera tricks, not effects.

whyItMatters: 'Feels like a Michel Gondry movie' is shorthand for handmade and dreamlike — a reference clients get instantly.

title: Nan Goldin
summary: American photographer (b. 1953) who made an intimate, flash-lit diary of her friends, lovers and nightlife.
characteristics: Diaristic snapshots of real lives and relationships
Saturated color, flash and available light
Tenderness and bruises side by side

examples.title: The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1985)
examples.detail: A slideshow-turned-book of her circle in New York.

examples.title: Nan One Month After Being Battered (1984)
examples.detail: A self-portrait that refuses to look away.

examples.title: All the Beauty and the Bloodshed (2022)
examples.detail: Laura Poitras's documentary about her art and activism; it won Venice's Golden Lion.

whyItMatters: Goldin shows that flash can be tender, not just harsh. She's the reference for intimacy that feels real.

title: Martin Parr
summary: British documentary photographer known for saturated, flash-lit satire of everyday leisure.
characteristics: Humor about tourism, food and consumer life

examples.title: The Last Resort (1986)
examples.detail: Working-class holidaymakers in New Brighton, in loud color.

examples.title: Common Sense (1999)
examples.detail: Close-ups of food, fake tans and souvenirs.

whyItMatters: Parr is proof that garish can be smart. If you like flash plus loud color, his close-ups are the vocabulary.

title: Angelo Badalamenti
summary: American composer (1937–2022) behind the dreamy, ominous sound of David Lynch's films.
characteristics: Jazz-noir bass lines and soft drums
Space and reverb around every note

examples.title: Blue Velvet (1986)
examples.detail: His first Lynch score, including 'Mysteries of Love' with Julee Cruise.

examples.title: Twin Peaks theme (1990)
examples.detail: The sound of a small town at night.

examples.title: Mulholland Drive (2001)
examples.detail: Lush and uneasy, like a love theme going wrong.

whyItMatters: If your songs feel like 2am, Badalamenti wrote the template: slow, beautiful and slightly wrong.

title: Mazzy Star
summary: American dream-pop band formed in 1989 by singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist David Roback.
characteristics: Slow tempos and weeping slide guitar
Reverb that makes songs feel far away

examples.title: She Hangs Brightly (1990)
examples.detail: Their debut: psychedelic folk in slow motion.

examples.title: 'Fade Into You' (1993)
examples.detail: The slow-dance ballad that defined them.

examples.title: Seasons of Your Day (2013)
examples.detail: A comeback after 17 years that sounded like no time had passed.

whyItMatters: 'Feels like Mazzy Star' tells anyone you mean slow, hushed and drenched in reverb.

title: Wong Kar-wai
summary: Hong Kong filmmaker (b. 1958) known for lush, melancholy films about longing and missed connections.
characteristics: Voice-over and pop songs on repeat
Longing, and timing that's always a little off

examples.title: Chungking Express (1994)
examples.detail: Two lonely cops, neon Hong Kong, 'California Dreamin'' on loop.

examples.title: Fallen Angels (1995)
examples.detail: Night-time Hong Kong through a wide-angle lens.

examples.title: In the Mood for Love (2000)
examples.detail: Two neighbors, narrow corridors and restraint.

whyItMatters: Wong Kar-wai is the reference for 'romantic and lonely at once' — color, blur and longing.

title: George Nakashima
summary: American woodworker and architect (1905–1990) famous for walnut furniture that keeps the tree's natural edge.
characteristics: Live, natural edges left on thick slabs

examples.title: Conoid Chair (c. 1960)
examples.detail: A cantilevered chair balanced on two runners.

examples.title: Minguren tables
examples.detail: Free-edge walnut slabs on sculpted bases.

examples.title: Altar for Peace (1986)
examples.detail: A walnut slab altar at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, New York.

whyItMatters: Nakashima turns 'I like wood' into something specific: walnut, live edges and visible joinery.

title: Isamu Noguchi
summary: Japanese-American sculptor and designer (1904–1988) whose paper lamps and organic furniture blur art and design.

examples.title: Akari light sculptures (from 1951)
examples.detail: Paper-and-bamboo lamps made in Gifu, Japan.

examples.title: Noguchi coffee table (1947)
examples.detail: A glass top resting on two interlocking wooden legs.

examples.title: The Noguchi Museum (1985)
examples.detail: His own museum and garden in Queens, New York.

whyItMatters: Noguchi's Akari lamps are a masterclass in warm, low, diffused light — the opposite of a ceiling fixture.

title: flash photography
summary: Photography lit by a burst of flash fired from the camera — the snapshot look of parties, paparazzi and 90s fashion.
era: From 1930s press cameras to 90s fashion and today's party pictures
characteristics: Subject bright, background falling into black
Hard shadows right behind the subject
The feeling of being caught in the moment

examples.title: Weegee — Naked City (1945)
examples.detail: Flash-lit New York crime scenes and nightlife.

examples.title: Nan Goldin — The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1985)
examples.detail: Friends and lovers in flash-lit rooms.

whyItMatters: Calling it 'flash photography' lets you brief a photographer precisely instead of saying 'that raw look'.

title: 90s rave flyer
summary: The graphic language of flyers for UK and US raves in the late 80s and 90s: loud, dense and made fast.
characteristics: Early computer graphics: chrome type, 3D, clip art
Every inch crammed with line-ups and info

examples.title: Shoom smiley flyers (1988)
examples.detail: Danny Rampling's London club helped make the acid-house smiley a symbol.

examples.title: Fantazia flyers (early 1990s)
examples.detail: Airbrushed fantasy art for giant UK raves.

examples.title: The Designers Republic for Warp Records (1990s)
examples.detail: The Sheffield studio that turned rave graphics into high design.

whyItMatters: It's shorthand for chaotic, joyful and loud. Saying '90s rave flyer' hands a designer a whole palette and energy.

title: mid-century modern
summary: Design from roughly 1945–1970: clean lines, organic curves, warm woods and furniture that sits low.
characteristics: Walnut and teak with visible grain
Low, horizontal furniture on tapered legs
Organic curves next to clean geometry
Big windows linking inside and outside

examples.title: Eames Lounge Chair and Ottoman (1956)
examples.detail: Molded plywood and leather by Charles and Ray Eames.

examples.title: Hans Wegner's Wishbone Chair (1949)
examples.detail: A Danish icon with a Y-shaped back.

examples.title: Case Study Houses (1945–1966)
examples.detail: Experimental Los Angeles homes of glass and steel.

whyItMatters: 'Mid-century modern' gives an interior designer a whole era to pull from — walnut, low lines, warm light.

title: Tokyo jazz kissa
summary: A Japanese jazz café where people come to listen to records on a serious sound system, usually in dim, wood-lined rooms.
era: Since the 1930s; peak 1950s–70s; a global listening-bar revival since the 2010s
characteristics: Walls of records and big speakers
Dark wood and low, warm light — no glare

examples.title: Chigusa, Yokohama (since 1933)
examples.detail: One of Japan's oldest jazz kissa.

examples.title: Jazz Kissa Basie, Ichinoseki (since 1970)
examples.detail: Famous for its obsessively tuned sound.

examples.title: Listening bars worldwide (2010s–)
examples.detail: London, New York and beyond borrowed the format.

whyItMatters: The perfect reference for rooms built around warmth and attention — dim, wooden, made for listening.

title: 70s conversation pit
summary: A sunken seating area built into the floor, designed to pull people together to talk.
era: Popular from the late 1950s through the 1970s
characteristics: Seating below floor level, wrapping around
Cozy enclosure inside an open room

examples.title: Miller House, Columbus, Indiana (1958)
examples.detail: Eero Saarinen and Alexander Girard's famous sunken living room.

examples.title: Togo sofa (1973)
examples.detail: Michel Ducaroy's floor-hugging sofa carries the same spirit.

examples.title: Modern revivals
examples.detail: Recent homes and hotels are bringing the pit back.

whyItMatters: It tells a designer you want seating that encloses you and lowers the room's center of gravity.

title: dream pop
summary: An atmospheric strain of alternative rock where vocals and guitars dissolve into reverb, like music heard half-asleep.
characteristics: Heavy reverb and echo on everything

examples.title: Cocteau Twins — Heaven or Las Vegas (1990)
Mazzy Star — So Tonight That I Might See (1993)
Beach House — Bloom (2012)
examples.detail: Dream pop for a new generation.

whyItMatters: If your songs swim in reverb, 'dream pop' is the genre word that gets you better recommendations.

title: brutalism
summary: Architecture from the 1950s–70s built from raw, exposed concrete in massive, blocky forms.
characteristics: Raw concrete (béton brut) with board marks

examples.title: Barbican Estate, London (1965–1976)
examples.detail: Towers, terraces and lakes in concrete.

examples.title: Boston City Hall (1968)
examples.detail: A civic building as a concrete sculpture.

whyItMatters: Brutalism is about weight and honesty. The word lets you ask for 'raw and monumental' instead of 'kind of concrete-y'.

title: Memphis design
summary: A Milan design collective (1981–1987) whose loud colors, squiggles and laminates broke the rules of good taste on purpose.

examples.title: Nathalie Du Pasquier's patterns
examples.detail: Bold prints that defined the look.

whyItMatters: 'Memphis' is instant shorthand for playful, clashing color — useful when 'fun' is too vague.

title: harsh flash lighting
summary: Light from a flash fired straight at the subject from the camera — hard, flat and unforgiving.
characteristics: Flat, bright faces with little modeling
Hard, dark shadows just behind the subject
Backgrounds that fall off into black

examples.title: Juergen Teller campaigns
examples.detail: Fashion shot like a family snapshot.

encounter: Fashion editorials, nightlife photography, album covers — any photo taken with the camera's built-in flash.
whyItMatters: It's the difference between 'raw' and 'lit': say 'direct on-camera flash' and a photographer knows what to bring.

title: distorted proportions
summary: Bodies, faces or objects deliberately stretched, squashed or warped away from their natural proportions.
characteristics: Heads or features too big or too small
Wide-angle or fisheye warping near the edges
encounter: Surrealist photography, fashion editorials, album art and experimental music videos.
whyItMatters: Distortion makes the familiar strange. Naming it lets you ask for 'stretched proportions' instead of 'something weird'.

title: acidic color
summary: Sharp, sour, high-saturation hues — acid green, chartreuse, lemon, hot pink — that feel almost toxic.
characteristics: Colors that feel artificial on purpose

examples.title: Charli XCX — brat (2024)
examples.detail: The lime-green cover that became a whole summer's aesthetic.

encounter: Streetwear drops, club posters, album covers and energy-drink packaging.
whyItMatters: Color is where 'I like bold' gets vague. 'Acidic' tells a designer sour and synthetic, not just bright.

title: film grain
summary: The fine, speckled texture in photos and films shot on film stock, from tiny light-sensitive crystals.
characteristics: A visible sandy texture, strongest in shadows
More pronounced with fast, high-ISO film
Adds warmth and a sense of 'real'

examples.title: 16mm film
examples.detail: The grainy look of indie films and music videos.

encounter: Street photography, indie film, fashion campaigns and filters that fake the look.
whyItMatters: Grain is texture you can ask for: 'shoot on film' or 'add grain' changes how honest an image feels.

title: fisheye lens
summary: An ultra-wide lens that sees up to about 180° and bends straight lines into curves.
characteristics: Strong barrel distortion — the world bulges
Whatever is closest to the lens looks huge

examples.title: 90s skate videos
examples.detail: Shot on a Sony VX1000 with a fisheye to get right up to the board.

examples.title: Action cameras
examples.detail: The default ultra-wide look of GoPro-style footage.

encounter: Skate culture, hip-hop videos, action cams and peephole views.
whyItMatters: Fisheye is one of the fastest routes to distortion. It lets you ask for 'VX1000 fisheye energy'.

title: hand-drawn mixed media
summary: Artwork that combines drawing with other materials — collage, paint, photos, tape, found paper.
characteristics: Layers of cut paper and photographs
Different textures colliding on one surface

examples.title: Hannah Höch — Cut with the Kitchen Knife… (1919–20)
examples.detail: A Dada photomontage of Weimar Germany.

encounter: Zines, album art, gig posters and editorial illustration.
whyItMatters: It names the handmade feeling you like, so you can ask for 'hand-drawn mixed media' instead of 'less digital'.

title: direct eye contact
summary: A subject looking straight into the camera, meeting the viewer's gaze.
characteristics: The subject looks back at you
Makes the viewer part of the picture

examples.title: Diane Arbus — Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey (1967)
Rineke Dijkstra — Beach Portraits (1990s)
examples.detail: Teenagers facing the camera on beaches.

encounter: Portrait photography, fashion campaigns and documentary work.
whyItMatters: Eye contact decides who's in control of a picture. A small detail that changes the whole feeling.

title: motion blur
summary: Streaks created when the subject or the camera moves while the shutter is open.
characteristics: A sense of speed or chaos
Sharp and blurred at once when mixed with flash

examples.title: Ernst Haas's color motion photographs (1950s)
examples.detail: Rodeo and bullfight scenes as pure movement.

examples.title: Dragging the shutter at parties
examples.detail: Slow shutter plus flash: sharp faces, streaking lights.

encounter: Nightlife photos, sports, music videos and long-exposure street shots.
whyItMatters: Blur can mean energy or dream. Asking to 'drag the shutter' gets you both at once.

title: risograph
summary: A stencil-based printer from Japan that prints one spot color at a time, giving grainy, vivid, slightly misaligned prints.
characteristics: Bright spot inks like fluorescent pink

examples.title: Gig posters and café menus
examples.detail: Short runs in two or three colors.

encounter: Zines, posters, indie book fairs and packaging that wants to feel handmade.
whyItMatters: 'Riso' is a precise word for that grainy two-color print look — printers know exactly what you mean.

title: chiaroscuro
summary: Strong contrast between light and dark, used to model form and add drama.
era: Renaissance and Baroque painting; later film noir

examples.title: Caravaggio — The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600)
examples.detail: A beam of light picks out a man in a dark room.

examples.title: Rembrandt — The Night Watch (1642)
examples.detail: A crowd sculpted by light and shadow.

encounter: Portrait lighting, noir films and moody product photography.
whyItMatters: It gives you a word for the drama you like in light — useful with photographers and lighting designers.

title: ring flash
summary: A circular flash that wraps around the lens, lighting the subject evenly from the front.
characteristics: A soft dark halo on the wall behind

examples.title: Martin Parr — Common Sense (1999)
examples.detail: Food and faces in unforgiving close-up.

encounter: Fashion, beauty close-ups, macro and medical photography.
whyItMatters: Ring flash is a step beyond 'flash' — know it and you can ask for that glossy, shadowless look.

title: caramel
summary: A sweet, browned-sugar note in wine, usually from toasted oak barrels or long aging.
characteristics: Seems sweet even in a dry wine
Often arrives with vanilla and toast

examples.title: Tawny Port
examples.detail: Aged in wood until it tastes of nuts and caramel.

examples.title: Rioja Gran Reserva
examples.detail: Long oak aging brings toffee and vanilla.

examples.title: Oaked Napa Cabernet
examples.detail: New barrels add caramel and mocha.

encounter: Oak-aged reds, fortified wines, aged rum and bourbon.
whyItMatters: 'Caramel' tells a sommelier you like oak and age — they can steer you to it instantly.

title: toasted oak
summary: Flavors a wine picks up from barrels whose insides were toasted over fire.
characteristics: Toast, coffee and smoke on the nose
Strongest in wines aged in new barrels

examples.title: Bourbon (charred new oak)
examples.detail: The same wood magic in whiskey.

encounter: 'Aged in new oak' on a label, barrel-fermented Chardonnay, most bourbons.
whyItMatters: Oak is one of the biggest choices a winemaker makes. Say 'toasted oak' and you've narrowed the shelf by half.

title: leather
summary: In wine, a savory aroma of worn leather that develops with age; in rooms, the material itself — warm, patinated and tactile.
characteristics: Appears as reds age and fruit fades
In interiors: leather that darkens and softens with use
Pairs naturally with tobacco and wood

examples.title: Aged Barolo
examples.detail: Tar and roses first — leather with time.

examples.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
examples.detail: Herbs, spice and leather in older bottles.

examples.title: Eames Lounge Chair
examples.detail: Leather that gets better as it wears.

encounter: Aged reds, club chairs, old libraries and well-worn bags.
whyItMatters: It shows up in both your wines and your rooms — a thread that ties your taste together.

title: vanilla
summary: A sweet, creamy aroma in wine that mostly comes from oak barrels — the same compound as in vanilla beans, vanillin.
encounter: Oaked reds, bourbon — and, famously, old books.
whyItMatters: Vanilla is a clue to the barrel. If you like it, ask for American oak.

title: tobacco
summary: An aroma of dried tobacco leaf or cigar boxes that emerges in aged reds.

examples.title: Aged Pauillac
examples.detail: 'Cigar box' is a classic Pauillac note.

encounter: Aged Bordeaux, Rioja and Cabernet — and many fragrances.
whyItMatters: Tobacco says you like age and savory depth over fresh fruit.

title: dark cherry
summary: A ripe, deep cherry fruit note — one of the core fruit flavors in many reds.
characteristics: Pairs with chocolate or spice notes
Fades toward dried fruit with age
encounter: Sangiovese, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Zinfandel.
whyItMatters: Fruit notes tell you where on the ripeness scale you like to sit.

title: smoke
summary: A campfire-like note from heavily toasted barrels, certain grapes like Syrah, or volcanic soils.
characteristics: Campfire, bacon fat or struck match
Often with black pepper in Syrah

examples.title: Lapsang souchong tea
examples.detail: Pine-smoked tea, the same campfire note.

encounter: Syrah, heavily oaked wines, peated whisky and smoked teas.
whyItMatters: Smoke is half of your 'campfire library' — a note you can ask for by name.

title: dried fig
summary: A rich, jammy dried-fruit note found in ripe or aged reds and wines made from dried grapes.

examples.title: Amarone della Valpolicella
examples.detail: Made from grapes dried for months.

examples.title: Aged Zinfandel
examples.detail: Ripe fruit turning to dried fruit.

encounter: Amarone, Port and aged warm-climate reds.
whyItMatters: Dried fruit means depth and warmth — useful when 'something rich' is too vague.

title: velvety tannins
summary: Tannins — the drying grip in red wine — that feel plush and smooth rather than rough.
encounter: Merlot, Grenache blends and older bottles.
whyItMatters: Texture is taste too. 'Velvety' tells someone you want comfort, not grip.

title: walnut wood
summary: A dark brown hardwood with a rich, chocolatey color and flowing grain — the signature wood of mid-century furniture.
characteristics: A warm glow under oil finishes
Pairs with brass, leather and linen

examples.title: Eames Lounge Chair (1956)
examples.detail: Today most often made with walnut veneer.

encounter: Mid-century furniture, record consoles, paneled dens and high-end kitchens.
whyItMatters: Walnut is specific where 'wood' isn't. Tell a designer 'walnut' and the whole palette follows.

title: low-profile seating
summary: Sofas and chairs that sit close to the floor, with low backs and deep seats.
characteristics: Makes ceilings feel higher and rooms calmer

examples.title: Togo sofa (Michel Ducaroy, 1973)
examples.detail: Folded foam that hugs the floor.

encounter: Mid-century living rooms, 70s lounges, Japanese interiors and hotel lobbies.
whyItMatters: Low seating changes a room's posture. It's the ingredient behind 'relaxed' in your rooms.

title: warm directional lighting
summary: Light from specific low sources — lamps, sconces, candles — in warm tones, creating pools of light and shadow.
characteristics: Light from the side or below eye level
Pools of light with soft shadow between
Several small sources instead of one big one

examples.title: Tokyo jazz kissa
examples.detail: Pools of light over dark wood.

examples.title: Chiaroscuro in Baroque painting
examples.detail: The painterly version: light from one side.

encounter: Bars, hotel lounges, restaurants — any room lit only by lamps.
whyItMatters: This is the real ingredient behind 'cozy.' Say it to a designer and they'll plan lamps, not downlights.

title: no overhead lights
summary: Lighting a room with lamps, sconces and candles instead of a central ceiling fixture.
characteristics: No harsh top-down light on faces
Several low sources at different heights

examples.title: Scandinavian hygge
examples.detail: Candles and lamps through dark winters.

examples.title: The 'big light' debate
examples.detail: The viral case against the ceiling light.

encounter: Cozy apartments, bars, restaurants and any evening routine that dims down.
whyItMatters: A rule you can hand to anyone lighting your space: keep light low and local.

title: linen
summary: A textile woven from flax fibers — slubby, matte and relaxed, with natural wrinkles.
characteristics: Wrinkles that read as relaxed, not messy
Natural oatmeal, sand and stone colors

examples.title: Linen bedding
examples.detail: Cool, and softer with every wash.

encounter: Bedding, curtains, slipcovers and summer clothes.
whyItMatters: Linen is the texture of 'calm.' It softens rooms full of wood and leather.

title: brass accents
summary: Small touches of brass — lamps, hardware, frames — that add warm metallic glints.

examples.title: Cabinet hardware
examples.detail: Small pulls that warm up walnut.

encounter: Lighting, hardware, bar fittings and picture frames.
whyItMatters: Brass is how warm rooms sparkle without turning cold or shiny.

title: minor keys
summary: Music built on minor scales, whose lowered third gives a darker, sadder or tenser color.
characteristics: A lowered third (and often sixth and seventh)
Common in ballads, noir and film scores
Can still groove — think trip hop and soul

examples.title: Chopin's Nocturnes
examples.detail: Many in minor keys, made for night.

examples.title: 'Autumn Leaves'
examples.detail: The jazz standard, often played in G minor.

encounter: Film scores, ballads, noir jazz and trip hop.
whyItMatters: 'Minor key' is the technical word for the sadness you keep saving.

title: 90–100 BPM
summary: A relaxed tempo of 90 to 100 beats per minute — around a slow walk or an easy head-nod.
characteristics: Common in hip-hop, R&B and trip hop

examples.title: Boom-bap hip-hop
examples.detail: Many classic 90s beats sit right around here.

encounter: Tap along to a song you love, or look up its BPM in a music app.
whyItMatters: Tempo is taste you can measure. Knowing your range makes playlists and briefs precise.

title: brushed drums
summary: Drums played with wire brushes instead of sticks — soft swishes and gentle taps.
characteristics: A swishing, circular sound on the snare

examples.title: Ed Thigpen with the Oscar Peterson Trio

encounter: Jazz ballads, bossa nova, lounge and quiet indie songs.
whyItMatters: Brushes are why some songs feel close. Ask for them when you want softness with a pulse.

title: breathy female vocal
summary: A singing style where you hear air in the voice — soft, close and intimate.
characteristics: Low in volume, high in intimacy
encounter: Bossa nova, dream pop, trip hop and film soundtracks.
whyItMatters: Vocal texture is a big part of taste. 'Breathy' tells a producer exactly the closeness you like.

title: reverb-heavy
summary: Music with lots of reverberation — the echoing tail that makes sound feel like it's in a big space.
characteristics: Long, washy tails after each note
Instruments that sound far away or dreamy

examples.title: Plate reverb on 60s records
examples.detail: The EMT 140 plate shaped countless classics.

encounter: Dream pop, shoegaze, ambient, film scores — and any cathedral.
whyItMatters: 'Swimming in reverb' is a core ingredient — it's what makes a song feel like 2am.

title: tape hiss
summary: The soft high-frequency noise of analog tape, now loved as a sign of warmth and lo-fi intimacy.
characteristics: A gentle, constant 'shhh' under the music
Often paired with warble and wow

examples.title: 4-track cassette recording
examples.detail: The Tascam Portastudio (1979) put a studio in the bedroom.

encounter: Cassettes, lo-fi playlists, vintage recordings and plugins that fake it.
whyItMatters: Hiss is to sound what grain is to images — imperfection that makes it feel real.

title: upright bass
summary: The large acoustic bass of jazz and folk — woody, round and plucked by hand.
characteristics: Sits under the music like a heartbeat

examples.title: Ron Carter
examples.detail: One of the most-recorded jazz bassists ever.

encounter: Jazz trios, folk, rockabilly and film-noir scores.
whyItMatters: Upright bass is warmth in the low end — part of why your songs feel acoustic and close.

title: Rhodes piano
summary: An electro-mechanical piano with a bell-like, warm tone — the sound of 70s soul and late-night jazz.

examples.title: Stevie Wonder — 'You Are the Sunshine of My Life' (1972)
Billy Joel — 'Just the Way You Are' (1977)

encounter: Soul, jazz fusion, neo-soul and lo-fi beats.
whyItMatters: Rhodes is the instrument behind 'warm and nostalgic' in your songs.

title: uncomfortable
summary: Work designed to hold tension rather than please — you look twice because something feels off.
characteristics: Too close, too bright, too still
Humor sitting right next to unease

examples.title: Diane Arbus's portraits (1960s)
examples.detail: Ordinary people made strange by a direct gaze.

encounter: Fashion editorials, art photography and design that breaks polish on purpose.
whyItMatters: Discomfort is a valid taste. Naming it helps you defend work that's meant to unsettle.

title: uneasy
summary: A quieter cousin of discomfort: a slow, creeping sense that something isn't right.
characteristics: Slow pacing and a low hum

examples.title: Twin Peaks (1990)
examples.detail: A small town with something wrong beneath it.

examples.title: Gregory Crewdson — Beneath the Roses (2003–2008)
examples.detail: Staged suburban scenes, cinematic and eerie.

encounter: Suburban photography, slow cinema and ambient soundtracks.
whyItMatters: 'Uneasy' is more precise than 'dark' — tension without shock.

title: electric
summary: A charged, high-energy feeling — nightlife, neon and a crowd about to erupt.
characteristics: A sense that something is happening now
encounter: Club photography, music videos, sports and fashion shows.
whyItMatters: Electric is energy you can brief: flash, color and motion.

title: off-kilter
summary: Slightly wrong balance — tilted horizons, odd crops and asymmetry that keep the eye unsettled.

examples.title: William Eggleston — The Red Ceiling (1973)
examples.detail: An everyday room from a strange angle.

encounter: Cinematography, editorial layouts and street photography.
whyItMatters: Off-kilter is about composition, not content — useful when you're briefing framing.

title: late-night
summary: The after-hours mood: artificial light, empty streets, intimacy and a little loneliness.
characteristics: Pools of artificial light in darkness

examples.title: Edward Hopper — Nighthawks (1942)
examples.detail: A lit diner on an empty street.

examples.title: Wong Kar-wai — Chungking Express (1994)
examples.detail: Snack bars and neon at closing time.

encounter: Night photography, noir films, slow jams and city walks.
whyItMatters: It runs through your saves — the thread between your images and your songs.

title: warm
summary: Warmth in taste: amber and brown tones, low light, round flavors and soft textures.
characteristics: Materials that feel good to touch

examples.title: Candlelit rooms
examples.detail: Light at the warm end of the scale.

encounter: Interiors, wine, photo grading and music production.
whyItMatters: Warm is a feeling you can back up with ingredients — lamp light, walnut, oak, caramel.

title: cozy
summary: Comfort through enclosure, softness and low light — the feeling of being held by a place.
encounter: Cafés, cabins, bars and bedrooms in winter.
whyItMatters: 'Cozy' is where most people stop. Your ingredients say what cozy means to you.

title: brooding
summary: Dark, serious and contemplative — intensity that simmers rather than shouts.
encounter: Wine, portraiture, noir films and minor-key music.
whyItMatters: Brooding tells people you like depth over brightness.

title: calm
summary: Quiet, low-stimulus and restful — spaces and works that let you exhale.

examples.title: Brian Eno — Music for Airports (1978)
examples.detail: Ambient music built to calm a room.

encounter: Spas, galleries, ambient music and bedrooms.
whyItMatters: Calm is a design goal you can measure: fewer sources of light, sound and clutter.

title: intimate
summary: Closeness — the feeling of being let into something small and private.

examples.title: Close-miked vocals
examples.detail: Singers who sound like they're next to you.

encounter: Portraits, small venues, handwritten notes and bedroom recordings.
whyItMatters: Intimacy connects your rooms and your songs — closeness is part of your taste.

title: melancholy
summary: A bittersweet sadness that's pleasurable to sit in.

examples.title: Wong Kar-wai — In the Mood for Love (2000)
Mazzy Star
examples.detail: Sad songs that feel like comfort.

encounter: Film, poetry, slow songs and autumn.
whyItMatters: Melancholy isn't just sad — it's a mood you can design for.

title: hazy
summary: Soft focus and blurred edges — in sound or image — as if seen through fog or memory.
characteristics: Reverb, hiss and washes in sound
encounter: Shoegaze, dream pop, film photography and nostalgic ads.
whyItMatters: Haze is texture as mood. It links your love of reverb with your love of grain.

title: campfire library
summary: A tasting metaphor: woodsmoke plus the vanilla-and-almond smell of old books.
encounter: Wine notes, whisky tastings, perfume and candle descriptions.
whyItMatters: Metaphors like this bridge feelings and ingredients — friends get it, sommeliers can decode it.

title: grandpa's leather armchair
summary: A metaphor for worn leather, pipe tobacco and polished wood — comfort with age on it.
encounter: Tasting notes, interiors and fragrance.
whyItMatters: Your shorthand for savory and aged — pass it to a sommelier along with 'leather, tobacco'.

title: old bookshop
summary: The smell of old paper, which chemists trace to aging paper releasing vanilla- and almond-like compounds.

examples.title: Aged Nebbiolo
examples.detail: Dried roses, tar and old-paper notes.

examples.title: Paper Passion perfume (2012)
examples.detail: A fragrance built on the smell of books.

encounter: Wine notes, fragrance and any second-hand bookshop.
whyItMatters: A reference like this makes your taste instantly shareable with non-experts.

title: 2am drive home
summary: A reference for music that feels like empty roads, streetlights and your own thoughts.
characteristics: Synths or soft guitars under streetlights

examples.title: Kavinsky — 'Nightcall' (2010)
examples.detail: Made famous by the film Drive (2011).

examples.title: 80s Japanese city pop
examples.detail: Glossy songs built for night cruising.

encounter: Driving playlists, film soundtracks and headphones on the night bus.
whyItMatters: It's the feeling your songs share — a reference anyone can picture.
